mitigation_mechanism: Rewetting drained peat — blocking canals so the water table rises — works on the fuel. Restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peatland is stated to reduce fire risk through increased moisture in surface and below-ground fire fuels (ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3), and improved hydrology after canal blocking is given as a route to reduced fire hazard (ev_fire_hazard_ritz13_4). Most of the cell describes the hazard from the loss side and the engine reads rewetting as the reversal of that chain: drainage and degradation made peat vulnerable to fire (ev_fire_hazard_bonn16_1); cleared, drained and replanted peat domes become vulnerable to wildfires that, once started, can burn for years (ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1); the drier conditions following drainage increase the risk of fire (ev_wgy_ram_14); and in a hotter, drier European climate the risk of forest and peat fires in drained peatlands is expected to increase further (ev_wgy_qa_8). A review of tropical peatland restoration techniques (Dohong et al.) adds that peatland rewetting also provides benefit in terms of reducing fire occurrences caused by dried out peatlands, citing Dohong and Lilia 2008, Page et al. 2009a and Panda et al. 2012 (ev_fire_hazard_doh18_1). The quantified result comes from a modelled fire-hazard index after large-scale canal-blocking rewetting in Riau, Sumatra: the frequency of continuous extreme-class hazard declined by 40% (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_1). Indonesian project accounts add field observations: in South Sumatra a revegetated project still survived large fires in 2015 and 2019, restoration in the area having restrained the spread of fires from nearby areas (ev_wet_fire_budi20_1); and in Riau 312 canal blocks over 6,060 ha of community land restored the hydrology of the peatland system and reduced the risk of wildfires (ev_wet_fire_terz22_1).
caveats: The drainage-fire chain is asserted, not measured. The European statements come from advocacy-adjacent sources — a question-and-answer brief drafted for the EU Nature Restoration Law negotiations (ev_wgy_qa_8) and the Ramsar technical guidance on peatland rewetting (ev_wgy_ram_14) — and the others from an introductory book chapter (ev_fire_hazard_bonn16_1) and a Ramsar briefing note (ev_wet_fire_hazard_ramsar18_1); none measures fire before and after rewetting, and the Dohong review restates the cited field studies rather than adding its own measurement (ev_fire_hazard_doh18_1). The restoration-frame claims are hedged as potential benefits, and Ritzema's is attributed to other studies rather than measured (ev_fire_hazard_mish21_3, ev_fire_hazard_ritz13_4). The quantified study models hazard from weather data checked against satellite hotspots, not burned area, and its other results are weaker or opposite: the area under extreme-class hazard was only 5% lower after rewetting (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_2); the mean duration of extreme events increased, with widespread prolonged extreme hazard occurring only in the drying El Niño years of 2015 and 2019 (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_3); and the authors conclude that duration was controlled by the weather and not influenced by rewetting (ev_fire_hazard_tauf23_4). In the severe dry years, when the widespread prolonged extreme hazard occurred, no benefit is visible. The authors also caution that La Niña years drive part of the decline, so the rewetting effect may be overstated. Provenance: Indonesian and Malaysian humid-tropical peat in upper-middle-income settings, plus guidance statements with no site; nothing was measured in a low-income or lower-middle-income country, and the benefit lands on the landscape and on society, not on a farmer's plot. The Indonesian project accounts carry no comparison area: the surviving Sumatran site is a single-site observation on land the authors describe as never fully rewetted (ev_wet_fire_budi20_1), and the Riau canal-block claim reports no fire data and comes from authors that include project staff (ev_wet_fire_terz22_1). The same Sumatran source records the other side at a neighbouring agro-sylvofishery project: trade-offs are increasing the vulnerability of peatland to fire, almost 50% of the area burned in the 2019 El Nino, and the causes of the fires are still being argued (ev_wet_fire_budi20_2) - a measured harm kept in the row, tied by the authors to liming peat for dryland crops and a fishery canal rather than to rewetting as such.

mitigation_mechanism: Flood peak and flood stage are different outcomes and this evidence moves them in different directions. Roughening and re-wetting the surface — re-vegetating bare peat, blocking gullies, lowering banks so water spreads onto a floodplain — slows storm-water delivery and cuts the discharge peak measured at or just below the works: 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N); 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); about 8% to 12% for a base-case modelled floodplain reconnection (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_2). A systematic review adds an average flood peak reduction of 30% for river and floodplain management, a bundle of measures of which floodplain and wetland restoration is a part (ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1). The loss frame agrees: bare peat gave higher peaks per unit rainfall (ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss) and embanking a floodplain raised the modelled downstream peak by 57% (ev_wetflA_acre_cherwell_embankment). mitigation_mechanism: Re-vegetating bare peat and blocking grips and gullies raises surface roughness and storage on the hillslope, so storm water is delivered more slowly. Peak discharge fell 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, both against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N), and 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); lag between peak rainfall and peak flow lengthened significantly at the re-vegetated site (ev_wetflA_shut_lag_O), restoration elsewhere produced lower discharge rates observable at drain and hill-stream level, with greater water-table stability and a reduction in peak flows (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_field), and modelling suggests drain blocking in blanket peat could reduce flood flows downstream (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_model). The loss frame points the same way: higher flood peaks and shorter times to peak go with peatland degradation and removal of vegetation cover (ev_wetflA_dads_degradation_loss, ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss). Peak and timing do not behave alike as storms grow — at the gully-blocked site the peak reduction held at 56% in the largest storms while the lag gain collapsed (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_largestorm_N, ev_wetflA_shut_lag_largestorm_N) — and at the rewetted gully the lag shortened even as the peak fell (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal). Restoration changed the timing and the peak of delivery but not the volume: the runoff coefficient was unchanged at both restored sites (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null). The starting state of the peat sets the sign of rewetting. After drainage, peak discharge is strongly reduced because the peat layer is no longer completely saturated (ev_wgy_ram_10) — so re-saturating moderately drained peat can raise peaks, peat that is already saturated having no capacity left to absorb a storm rather than storing it — whereas intensively drained and severely degraded peat soils increase peak rates again through water-repellent peat and stagnating soil horizons (ev_wgy_ram_11), and loss of Sphagnum cover and spread of bare peat can increase peak flow and shorten runoff lag (ev_wgy_ram_12); it is on those degraded sites that rewetting and revegetation can lower peaks.
caveats: The measurements are plot to micro-catchment; the catchment-scale benefit is not demonstrated. No effect was found at the scale of the entire 260 km2 catchment (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null), the influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null), the monitoring authors state that isolating restoration effects within empirical storm-flow datasets is problematic at the large catchment scale (ev_wetflA_shut_catchment_undetectable), and a realistic suite of land-management changes modelled against an extreme rainfall event gave a median flood-peak reduction of only 2% (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_model_2pct). Position decides the sign: upland wetlands tend to be flood-generating areas, frequently saturated with little water storage potential (ev_wetflA_acre_position_upland); blanket bogs close to saturation for most of the year rarely attenuate flow and are much more likely to contribute to storm runoff (ev_wetflA_acre_saturated_bog_reversal); a moorland scheme designed to delay runoff synchronised sub-catchment peaks and increased downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal); and an on-site storage gain can still raise peaks at catchment scale (ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment). Even on the hillslope the lever is conditional: ditch blocking in upland peat reduces flow peaks only in the steepest, smoothest drains, with the roughness of the surrounding vegetated peat mattering more than the ditches (ev_wetflA_dads_ditchblock_conditional), and upland ditches may increase or decrease local flood peaks depending on layout, topography and synchronisation (ev_wetflA_dads_ditch_sign_flip). The review covering this family reports moderate flood-reduction results but without empirical evidence for larger-scale effects (ev_wetflA_zhu_peatland_confidence). Retention is a favourable-setting claim, not a general property: the Ramsar guidance says peatlands may, in favourable settings, function as retention areas after rewetting, especially where unused or used for paludiculture and so less vulnerable to inundation (ev_wgy_ram_13) — storage of flood water, which is a stage and volume service, not a general reduction of peaks. mitigation_mechanism: Reconnecting and rewetting floodplain and depressional wetland puts storm water somewhere other than the channel. Modelled peak flow fell by up to 37% at the reach scale, and by up to 19% where banks were lowered furthest (ev_flood_hazard_feder22_1, ev_flood_hazard_feder22_6); wooded wetlands increase flood storage, reduce flood peaks and increase peak travel time (ev_wetflA_acre_wooded_wetland); depressional wetlands could store 72% of the total runoff volume of a 2-year rainfall event (ev_wetflA_acre_depression_storage); and in the loss frame, embanking a floodplain to remove its storage raised the modelled downstream peak by 57% (ev_wetflA_acre_cherwell_embankment). A systematic review adds an average flood peak reduction of 30% for river and floodplain management, a bundle of measures of which floodplain and wetland restoration is a part (ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1). Peak and stage are separate outcomes that move apart: removing the levees lowered cross-sectional water-surface elevation by an average of 0.66 m (ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_1) while decreasing peak discharge over the same segment by less than 0.04 to 0.13% (ev_flood_hazard_jacob15_3), and roughening the floodplain with shrubs and trees can double the size and depth of the inundated area for the same flood (ev_wetflA_acre_inundation_stage_up). Levee setbacks are where stage falls as well: a critical review of artificial-levee alteration (Knox et al.) reports reduced flood stages after a levee setback on the Missouri River in Iowa (Smith et al.) (ev_flood_hazard_knox22_1), a 50 cm flood peak reduction after a setback on the Elbe in Germany (Serra-Llobet et al.) (ev_flood_hazard_knox22_2), and 1 in 1250 year flood levels reduced by 0.3 m along the Dutch Rhine (Klijn et al., 2018) (ev_flood_hazard_knox22_4); reconnecting floodplains and channels along the Austrian Danube cut the flood peak by 110 m3s−1 per river kilometer (Hudson, 2021) (ev_flood_hazard_knox22_3). A weighted meta-analysis of the flow-regulation services of wetlands (Kadykalo et al. 2016) found that, consistent with conventional wisdom, on average wetlands reduce the frequency and magnitude of floods and increase flood return period (ev_flood_hazard_kad16_1).
caveats: The clear evidence is explicitly local and explicitly for moderate rainfall events (ev_wetflA_dads_summary_moderate); for the most extreme events, and at large catchment scales, the evidence does not suggest a major effect on downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_dads_summary_extreme_null, ev_wetflA_dads_largecatchment_null), during major catastrophic floods the presence or absence of wetlands has no effect (ev_wetflA_acre_catastrophic_null), and the storable share of a flood falls with rarity — the same depressional wetlands held 72% of the runoff volume of a 2-year event but 41% of a 100-year event (ev_wetflA_acre_depression_storage). At the catchment outlet the modelled changes are small: 0.65% off the Q100 peak, 1.1% off the Q25 peak, and no change in flood volume for the Q2 storm (ev_flood_hazard_worl23_2, ev_flood_hazard_worl23_3, ev_flood_hazard_worl23_4), with only modest peak attenuation across the design storms because of the steep, flashy setting (ev_flood_hazard_worl23_1); and the aggregated effects of multiple wetlands can differ considerably from the functions observed at individual wetland scale (ev_wetflA_thor_scale_mismatch). The sign flips with position: upstream wetland obviously amplified downstream flood risks while downstream wetland was the part the authors would restore first (ev_flood_hazard_wu23_4); restoring many reaches had no effect on property damages and some worsened inundation upstream through backwater effects (ev_flood_hazard_gour20_3, ev_flood_hazard_gour20_4); headwater wetlands fill during relatively normal summer rain, which spends the capacity they would need for a much larger event, whereas downstream wetlands that stay dry keep that buffering capacity (ev_flood_hazard_ahlen22_2, ev_flood_hazard_ahlen22_1). The same meta-analysis puts the empirical studies alone at a small overall mean effect size, wetlands reducing flooding,, a weighted overall mean correlation coefficient of 0.28, smaller than the modelling studies imply (ev_flood_hazard_kad16_2); and it pools existing wetlands against drained or absent ones rather than restored sites. The Knox case entries are second-hand table rows on large regulated rivers where a levee had cut the floodplain off (ev_flood_hazard_knox22_1, ev_flood_hazard_knox22_2). Rewetting itself consumes flood storage: raising ditch water levels to meet winter ecological targets cost flood-water storage equivalent to 3% of the median annual flood volume (ev_wetflA_acre_somerset_rewet_cost) — a wet wetland and an empty flood store are competing objectives. The 30% review average credits the whole river-and-floodplain bundle - river restoration, floodplain and wetland restoration, leaky barriers and offline storage - not wetland restoration alone; it is a peak, not a stage, figure from a corpus that is mostly European and largely British, and its statement that the reduction is larger in larger catchments sits against the catchment-scale nulls above (ev_flood_hazard_bagh25w1_1). Provenance: temperate and high-income, UK, US and Swedish, with a Chinese basin model; the sole lower-middle-income measurement in scope is a reversal, Zimbabwean headwater dambos protected because they are assumed to reduce floods but measured as the principal mechanism of storm-discharge generation (ev_wetflA_acre_dambo_reversal). The benefit is off-plot in every case.

The first treats waterlogging of neighbouring land as a risk to be managed; the second describes a setting where wetting neighbouring farmland is built into the method.
caveats: These are design constraints stated by an authority, not measurements. Neither statement says how often neighbouring land is waterlogged, by how much, for how long, or what it costs the farmers who work it, and both come from one advocacy-adjacent guidance document; they establish that the risk is recognised, not its size or frequency, and they should not be read as evidence that rewetting routinely floods farmland. Unlike the flood benefits elsewhere in this recipe, the cost here falls on the neighbouring farm household rather than downstream. For scoping, a rewetting proposal adjacent to farmland should plan for gradual water-level raising, identify the adjacent parcels whose water level the design may depend on, and treat any need to raise water on those parcels as something to agree with their users before the works, not an incidental side effect. No country, income group, climate zone or farming system is attached to either statement. mitigation_mechanism: Coastal wetland standing between a cyclone and exposed property reduces the damage done, measured as an elasticity across US Atlantic and Gulf coastal counties: a 1% loss of coastal wetlands is associated with a 0.6% increase in property damage (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_1). Valued at the margin, the median county's wetland is worth about $91,000 per km2 per year in storm protection, against an average of about $1.8 million and a range from less than $800 to $100 million per km2 (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_4), and a counterfactual on a single hurricane put the damage attributable to prior wetland loss at about $430 million (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_5). A farm-level observation points the same way: after a cyclone on the Queensland coast, croplands within 1 km of mangroves and tidal marshes showed reduced crop cover declines compared with more distant areas (ev_crop_yield_rowl26w1_2).
caveats: Protection is proportionately smallest where the storm is strongest: the elasticity of property damage with respect to wetlands is 0.58 for a tropical storm and 0.35 for a category 3 to 5 hurricane (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_2, ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_3). Built defences substitute for it — the elasticity is 0.50 in states with stricter building codes against 0.81 where codes and enforcement are weaker (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_6). All of this is measured on existing wetland cover rather than on a restoration project, and the same authors warn that a replacement wetland may take decades to fully develop the functions of the wetland it replaces (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_7), so the measured value is not what a new project delivers. The Queensland result is crop cover read from a satellite vegetation index, not yield, around existing mangrove and marsh that the authors could not separate, and the binary presence of a coastal wetland on the seaward side of a field did not contribute substantially to the models (ev_crop_yield_rowl26w1_3). Provenance: a US panel study of high-income coastal counties and an Australian satellite study; the US outcome is damage to coastal property, a societal and asset-owner benefit rather than a rural livelihood one, the Australian outcome is crop cover on farmland, and nothing in the cell speaks to a low-income or lower-middle-income coast.

mitigation_mechanism: The vulnerable asset is the canal dam that holds the water table up. In December 2005, after an extreme rainfall event, both dams in the Kalampangan Canal were damaged by water seeping underneath and along the sides; they were repaired in March 2006 and were damaged again in August 2006 (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_7). During an extreme rainfall event in August 2007 a further dam was damaged in a flash flood, the canal water level rising by several metres in a short period (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_8). The rainfall is the trigger; the vulnerability is structural, since highly permeable tropical peat lets seepage pass beneath and alongside a dam, and the sunken canals intercept overland and interflow, raising canal discharges when the rain is extreme.
caveats: This is a single demonstration site in Indonesian tropical peat, recorded as a case study rather than measured across projects, and the repeat failure after repair is the most transferable part of it. It says nothing about damage to the wetland itself, about coastal or temperate wetland types, or about water-control structures of other designs. Read it as a design and maintenance risk for canal-blocking programmes in deep permeable peat — dam siting relative to the contour, seepage control, and a repair budget that assumes recurrence — rather than as a general sensitivity of wetland management to extreme rainfall. Provenance: humid-tropical, upper-middle-income, with no comparable record from any other peat region.
